system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2118-05-17 23:37:00 to 2118-05-19 17:45:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A man with a history of cerebrovascular disease, coronary artery disease, and alcohol use was admitted for chest pain and dizziness. Initial evaluation ruled out acute cardiac ischemia with normal troponins and EKG. The chest pain was determined to be musculoskeletal. A non-contrast head CT showed no acute intracranial abnormalities, and his dizziness, described as lightheadedness, resolved with IV rehydration and was attributed to dehydration and alcohol use. He was monitored for alcohol withdrawal using the CIWA protocol and received thiamine, folic acid, and multivitamins. His tremor remained at baseline, and no new neurological deficits were found. He was discharged stable with instructions to avoid alcohol, continue all prescribed medications, and follow up with primary care, with plans for home support services.
problems: Coronary atherosclerosis of unspecified type of vessel, native or graft
Other and unspecified alcohol dependence, unspecified
Other late effects of cerebrovascular disease

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  A ___ male with chest pain.  Please evaluate for infiltrate,
effusion, or mediastinal abnormality.

FINDINGS:  A single AP portable upright chest radiograph is reviewed and
compared to ___.

Cardiomediastinal appearance is little changed, with evidence of prior median
sternotomy and CABG.  Atelectasis or scarring at the left base is unchanged. 
Lungs are otherwise clear.  There is no pleural effusion or pneumothorax. 
Pulmonary vascularity is normal.

IMPRESSION:  No acute cardiopulmonary process.  Chronic atelectasis or
scarring at the left base.

HISTORY:  ___ male with atypical chest pain, intermittent x1 week. The
pain described as being under left breast, sharp, worse with lying down.
Positive ETOH.  Positive D-dimer.  Please evaluate for PE, dissection or rib
fracture.

COMPARISON:  Chest x-ray from same day, and from ___.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT acquired axial imaging of the chest was performed before and
after administration of intravenous contrast via non-gated chest pain CTA
technique.  Multiplanar reformatted images were obtained and reviewed.

CTA CHEST:  There is no pulmonary embolism.  Thoracic aorta is normal in
caliber and contour throughout, without evidence of dissection.

Heart, pericardium and great vessels are normal.  There is no pleural or
pericardial effusion.  There is three-vessel coronary artery calcification.
Note is made of a dominant right vertebral artery with a diminutive left
vertebral artery. There is evidence of prior median sternotomy.

Multiple borderline enlarged small lymph nodes are seen scattered throughout
the mediastinum, and there is a likely calcified lymph node seen just superior
to the top of the aortic arch adjacent to the trachea, although this could
also represent volume averaging from adjacent aortic arch calcification.

There is streaky airspace opacity at the left lung base, which could represent
atelectasis versus aspiration, versus early infectious process.  There is mild
centrilobular emphysema, most prominent in the right upper lobe.  There is
mild right basilar atelectasis.

Limited views of the upper abdomen are notable for marked diffuse fatty
infiltration of the liver.

OSSEOUS STRUCTURES:  No suspicious lesions are seen.  There is no fracture.

IMPRESSION:
1.  No pulmonary embolism.  No aortic dissection.  No rib fractures.
2.  Streaky left basilar opacity could be consistent with atelectasis,
aspiration, or early infectious process.
3.  Three-vessel coronary artery calcifications.
4.  Multiple borderline enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes.
5.  Diffuse fatty infiltration of the liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve been having this chest pain on the left side. It’s been going on for about a week, gets worse when I lie down. Feels sharp, like it’s in my back too sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any shortness of breath with it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little, but not bad. No sweating or nausea. I did have a drink earlier today—vodka, about half a pint.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I notice you were here just a couple weeks ago for chest pain and dizziness. You mentioned you’ve been drinking regularly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I admit it. I drink every day. I know I shouldn’t, but I haven’t been feeling great since last time. The chest pain hasn’t gone away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And are you taking your heart medications—like aspirin, Plavix, the beta-blocker?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not always. Sometimes I forget. Or I just don’t feel like it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ll help you get back on track. For now, we’ve done some tests. Your EKG looks stable—no new heart damage. Your troponin, which checks for heart attack, is normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my heart again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Doesn’t look like it. The pain doesn’t act like typical heart pain—it’s not with exertion, and we can reproduce it when I press on your chest wall. That suggests it might be musculoskeletal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So like a muscle strain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. But we also did a CT scan because your D-dimer was high, which can sometimes mean a blood clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. Did I have a clot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, good news—the CT showed no pulmonary embolism or aortic dissection. But there is a small streaky area in your left lung base.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that pneumonia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be early pneumonia, or just atelectasis—collapsed air sacs, maybe from not breathing deeply. You don’t have a fever, your white count is normal, and you’re not coughing up anything. So we don’t think it’s serious infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do smoke a pipe every day. Could that be related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could contribute to the lung changes. But right now, we’re not starting antibiotics. We’ll watch your breathing and oxygen levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Chest pain’s a bit better. Still there, but not as bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. We checked your heart scan—the p-MIBI—and it shows normal blood flow and heart function. Ejection fraction is 62%, which is strong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my heart’s okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. No signs of blockages causing problems now. We’ll keep you on your usual meds—Plavix, aspirin, atorvastatin, metoprolol, and your thyroid pill.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the alcohol? I know you’re going to say stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I do. You’re at risk for withdrawal, so we’re giving you IV fluids, thiamine, folic acid, and multivitamins. You’re not showing signs of withdrawal now, so we don’t need sedatives like Valium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t get shakes or seizures. I’ve never had that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still, drinking daily puts strain on your heart, liver, and overall health. The CT showed fatty infiltration in your liver—that’s from alcohol and diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can lead to liver problems over time. But stopping alcohol helps reverse it. We’re also giving you a daily injection to prevent blood clots while you’re in the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. Your oxygen levels are stable, no fever, and your chest X-ray hasn’t changed. Still no signs of pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So when can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely tomorrow. We’ll make sure you’re pain-free and stable. We’re updating your discharge meds—adding a stronger stomach protector, pantoprazole, and keeping all your heart meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I saw two stomach meds on the list—pantoprazole and omeprazole. Do I need both?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good catch. You’ll take pantoprazole daily and keep omeprazole only if needed. We’ll clarify that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well overnight. No chest pain, vitals stable. We’re ready to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What do I need to do now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take all your medications as prescribed—especially aspirin, Plavix, and your statin. Stop drinking alcohol completely. Follow up with your primary doctor and cardiologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the chest pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use your nitroglycerin under the tongue. If it doesn’t go away in 5 minutes, call 911. Same for shortness of breath, nausea, or dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try to do better. I know I need to change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to support you. A home health nurse will check in to help with meds and follow-up. You’re going home with services to help you stay on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Let me get the discharge papers ready. You should be out by midday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Here’s your medication list and instructions. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it. Take meds, no drinking, call if something’s wrong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re doing the right thing. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, Doctor.

summary.summary_paragraph: A man with a history of coronary artery disease, prior CABG, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and alcohol use disorder was admitted for left-sided chest pain and alcohol intoxication. The chest pain was atypical for acute coronary syndrome, reproducible on exam, and serial troponins were negative. A p-MIBI stress test showed normal myocardial perfusion and ejection fraction of 62%. A CTA chest ruled out pulmonary embolism or dissection but showed a left basilar opacity, likely atelectasis or early pneumonia; however, the patient lacked fever, leukocytosis, or hypoxia, so antibiotics were not continued. He was monitored for alcohol withdrawal with supportive care including thiamine and multivitamins but did not require benzodiazepines. His pain resolved during the stay, and he was discharged asymptomatic on home medications with instructions to abstain from alcohol and follow up with primary and cardiology care. Home health services were arranged.
